papers.title_in_file: Enhancing GPU-acceleration in the Python-based Simulations of Chemistry Framework
papers.version_note: arXiv:2404.09452v2 (22 Jul 2024); the file name says Python-Based-Quantum-Chemistry-Calculations-with-GPU-Acceleration but the text is the paper the record names. The text layer holds the abstract paragraph twice and the NMR paragraph twice.
papers.what_it_is: An industrial (ByteDance Research) report of GPU4PySCF v1.0: GPU-accelerated density-fitted DFT, gradient, Hessian and solvent models in PySCF, with speed and cost benchmarks against Q-Chem 6.1 and application demos, all on classical hardware.

assertions.value: The authors state that, when performing DFT calculations on modern GPU platforms, GPU4PySCF delivers 30 times speedup over a 32-core CPU node, with approximately 90% cost savings for most DFT tasks.
quotes: GPU4PySCF delivers 30 times speedup over a 32-core CPU node, resulting in approximately 90% cost savings for most DFT tasks
assertions.reader_inference: The body text reports 20 times for SCF and 50 times for Hessian against Q-Chem 6.1 (Section 2.2); the single 30 times figure is not derived in the text, only in Figure 2, which is an image.

assertions.value: The authors state that GPU4PySCF now provides performance equivalent to that of 600-1000 CPU cores for running conventional CPU-based quantum chemistry software, and cost savings of up to 90% with NVIDIA A100-80G cards.
quotes: GPU4PySCF now provides performance that is equivalent to that of 600-1000 CPU cores for running conventional CPU-based quantum chemistry software.
it offers substantial cost savings, for instance, up to 90% when utilizing the NVIDIA A100-80G cards
assertions.reader_inference: The paper does not show how the 600-1000 core figure is derived; the benchmark in Section 2 compares one A100 with 32 CPU cores.

assertions.value: The authors state that, through their contributions, GPU4PySCF v1.0 can be regarded as a fully functional and industrially relevant platform, and that they recommend it for many industrial quantum chemistry applications.
quotes: GPU4PySCF v1.0 can now be regarded as a fully functional and industrially relevant platform
GPU4PySCF is natural choice that we can now recommend for many industrial quantum chemistry applications

assertions.value: The authors state that the performance calculations have been cross-validated with Q-Chem 6.1.
quotes: have been rigorously cross-validated with Q-Chem 6.1, ensuring reliability and accuracy
assertions.reader_inference: Appendices B to D give the energy, gradient and Hessian differences against Q-Chem 6.1 that support this statement.

assertions.value: The authors cite a 2018 NERSC workload analysis as stating that DFT algorithms account for 30% of total computational resource usage.
quotes: According to a 2018 workload analysis by the National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center (NERSC), DFT algorithms account for 30% of total computational resource usage

assertions.value: The authors state that when they started, GPU4PySCF contained CUDA kernels for 4-center two-electron integrals and GPU-accelerated direct SCF (Hartree-Fock), and that their contributions add density fitting (adapting the Rys quadrature kernels to 3-center quantities), tensor-core use for tensor contractions, and integration of open-source packages for DFT methods, basis sets, solvent models, properties, geometry optimization and transition state search.
quotes: GPU4PySCF contained CUDA kernels for 4-center two-electron integrals and GPU accelerated direct SCF (Hartree-Fock) functionality [20]
These adapt the Rys quadrature CUDA kernels in GPU4PySCF to the 3-center quantities for density fitting.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors describe the scope of their own contribution in Section 1.

assertions.value: The authors state that optimizing the codebase for modern GPU architectures such as tensor cores achieves up to twice the speed in tensor contractions.
quotes: to leverage modern GPU architectures, such as tensor cores, to achieve up to twice the speed in tensor contractions
assertions.reader_inference: No measurement of the tensor-core gain is shown in the text.

assertions.value: The authors state that the density fitting implementation is optimized for small to medium sized molecules, that it is efficient for molecules with less than 200 atoms, and that larger molecules (more than 168 atoms) are handled by the existing direct SCF scheme, which the paper does not focus on.
quotes: The density fitting implementation is optimized for small to medium sized molecules
This is efficient for small molecules with less than 200 atoms.
Larger molecules with more than 168 atoms can be calculated within the existing direct SCF scheme in GPU4PySCF [20], which we do not focus on here.

assertions.value: The authors report that the benchmark dataset has 13 small molecules with 20-168 atoms covering 8 elements (H, C, O, N, Mg, S, Cl, P), chosen from the supplement of a geometry optimization paper and two medium-sized molecules from another supplement.
assertions.anchor: Section 2.1, p.4; Appendix A, Table 5, p.27
quotes: The newly constructed dataset includes 8 elements (H, C, O, N, Mg, S, Cl, P), and 13 small molecules with 20-168 atoms.
assertions.certainty_reason: The dataset is defined in Section 2.1 and Table 5.
assertions.reader_inference: Section 2.1 says small molecules are those with fewer than 100 atoms, yet the dataset reaches 168 atoms; the 100-atom limit applies to the source supplement, not to the final dataset.

assertions.value: The authors report that the typical DFT protocol for timings is def2-TZVPP, B3LYP and (99,590) grids on NVIDIA A100-80G, with the def2-universal-JKFIT auxiliary basis in the scaling figure.
quotes: For a typical DFT protocol with def2-TZVPP, B3LYP, and (99,590) grids, we record the wall clock time for SCF, gradient, and Hessian calculations on NVIDIA A100-80G.
def2-TZVPP basis set, def2-universal-JKFIT auxiliary basis, B3LYP, (99,590) grids, on A100-80G.
assertions.certainty_reason: Setup stated in Section 2.1 and the Figure 1 caption.

assertions.value: The authors state that all benchmark computations in that section are conducted on closed-shell systems using density fitting, and that the benchmark covers three modules: SCF, gradient and Hessian.
quotes: In this section, all computations are conducted on closed-shell systems using density fitting.
Self-Consistent Field (SCF), gradient, and Hessian calculations.

assertions.value: The authors report wall clock times on one A100 GPU: for Vitamin C, the smallest molecule, SCF takes 1.7 seconds, gradient 0.68 seconds and Hessian 43 seconds; for Valinomycin, the largest molecule, SCF takes 309 seconds and gradient 58 seconds; the Hessian of Sphingomyelin (84 atoms) takes 30 minutes.
quotes: For the smallest molecule (Vitamin C) in the dataset, SCF, gradient, and Hessian take 1.7, 0.68, and 43 seconds respectively.
For the largest molecule (Valinomycin) in the dataset, SCF and gradient calculations take 309 seconds and 58 seconds respectively.
The Hessian calculation of Sphingomyelin (84 atoms) takes 30 minutes.
assertions.reader_inference: These are single-run wall clock times with no repeats or variance reported.

assertions.value: The authors report that coupled-perturbed SCF iterations for Azadirachtin, Taxol and Valinomycin do not converge, so Hessians are not available for those molecules.
quotes: Unfortunately, coupled-perturbed SCF iterations for (Azadirachtin, Taxol, Valinomycin) does not converge.

assertions.value: The authors state that SCF and gradient calculations scale quartically with system size and the Hessian scales as the fifth power of the system size (O of N to the fifth, printed flat in the text layer), and that the observed slope of the scaling curve decreases as the system gets larger due to sparsity.
quotes: Theoretically, SCF and gradient calculations are quartic scaling with respect to the system size, while Hessian calculation is O(N 5).
The slope of the scaling curve decreases as the system size gets larger, due to sparsity.

assertions.value: The authors state that the bottleneck for a large molecule is CPU memory storage, and that a CPU-GPU hybrid strategy stores GTO integrals: intermediates stay in GPU memory for small molecules and in CPU memory for large systems, transferred asynchronously to the GPU.
quotes: The bottleneck of calculating a large molecule is the CPU memory storage. A CPU-GPU hybrid strategy is employed to store GTO integrals in this work.
The data in CPU memory is asynchronously transferred to GPU memory for consumption.
assertions.certainty_reason: Design of the implementation, stated in Section 2.1.

assertions.value: The authors report that on average GPU4PySCF is 20 times faster than identical SCF calculations in Q-Chem 6.1 on 32 CPU cores, and that the speedup increases to 50 times for Hessian calculations, while the gradient speedup is relatively modest.
quotes: GPU4PySCF achieves a performance that is 20 times faster than identical SCF calculations performed using Q-Chem 6.1 on 32 CPU cores.
This speedup increases dramatically to 50 times for Hessian calculations
the acceleration observed in gradient calculations is relatively modest
assertions.reader_inference: The 50 times Hessian figure compares an analytic Hessian on the GPU against a finite-difference Hessian in Q-Chem (see the related assertion on the reference method), so it mixes an algorithm difference with a hardware difference.

assertions.value: The authors state that, because of a memory management issue in Q-Chem's density fitting coupled-perturbed SCF, the reference Hessians were computed by finite differences while GPU4PySCF computes them analytically, and that they expect resolving the issue could raise Q-Chem Hessian efficiency by a factor of 2-3.
quotes: the reference Hessian calculations are performed using finite difference methods. But the Hessian matrices are calculated analytically in GPU4PySCF.
We anticipate that resolving these issues could enhance the efficiency of Hessian calculations in Q-Chem by a factor of 2-3.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the limit of the Hessian comparison in Section 2.2.

assertions.value: The authors state that, given restricted access to commercial software, benchmarking is focused exclusively on Q-Chem, that Hessian benchmarks cover only molecules with 20-84 atoms, and that complete alignment of settings between packages is a significant challenge.
quotes: our benchmarking efforts are focused exclusively on Q-Chem, a prominent commercial platform
We only benchmark the speedup across molecules containing 20-84 atoms.
Achieving complete alignment between various quantum chemistry software settings presents a significant challenge.
assertions.certainty_reason: Limits of the comparison stated in Section 2.2.

assertions.value: The authors report that, from AWS pricing for comparable machinery, GPU4PySCF reduces expense by about 90% across most tasks, with the saving decreasing to 70% for the gradient calculation with pure DFT.
quotes: An evaluation of the actual costs based on AWS pricing for comparable machinery shows that GPU4PySCF can reduce expenses by about 90% across most tasks.
For the gradient calculation with pure DFT, the saving decreases to 70%.
assertions.reader_inference: Cost figures depend on the prices at one date and on how an 8-GPU instance is charged against one GPU.

assertions.value: The authors report the cost basis as $40.966 per hour for a p4de.24xlarge GPU instance (8 A100-80G GPUs, 96 vCPUs, 1152 GiB CPU memory) and $2.117 per hour for an r7i.8xlarge CPU instance (32 vCPUs, 256 GiB memory).
quotes: $40.966/hr for p4de.24xlarge GPU instance with 8 A100-80G GPUs, 96 vCPUs and 1152 GiB CPU memory.
$2.117/hr for r7i.8xlarge CPU instance with 32 vCPUs and 256 GiB memory.
assertions.certainty_reason: Cost inputs stated in the Figure 2 caption.
assertions.reader_inference: The text does not state how the 8-GPU instance price is divided for a one-GPU run.

assertions.value: The authors state that larger molecules typically experience a more substantial speedup than smaller ones, which they attribute to high GPU occupancy.
quotes: larger molecules typically experience a more substantial speedup compared to smaller molecules
This is due to the high GPU occupancy of a large molecule.

assertions.value: The authors state that the pure DFT gradient could technically be accelerated with a more efficient algorithm (a J matrix engine) and leave that implementation as future work.
quotes: be accelerated with a more efficient algorithm [23]. We leave this implementation as future work.

assertions.value: The authors report that with the A100-80G and density fitting, GPU4PySCF accelerates SCF by 40-80 times, gradient by 20-40 times and Hessian by 100-170 times for PCM solvent models, with molecules of up to 42 atoms evaluated, and that the SCF speedup of Vitamin C in the gas phase is around 33.
quotes: GPU4PySCF significantly accelerates the SCF calculations by 40-80 times, gradient calculations by 20-40 times, and Hessian calculations by 100-170 times, respectively.
For instance, the speedup of SCF for Vitamin C in gas phase is around 33.
We evaluate the performance of molecules with up to 42 atoms.
assertions.reader_inference: Table 1 lists Hessian speedups of 186.0 and 186.5 for Penicillin V, above the stated 100-170 range.

assertions.value: The authors report in the PCM speedup table, over Q-Chem on CPUs, the following (SCF, gradient, Hessian): Vitamin C, C-PCM 39.8 (SCF), 21.6 (gradient), 107.2 (Hessian), and IEF-PCM 31.0, 18.3, 100.1; Mg Porphin, C-PCM 86.8, 40.9, 168.5, and IEF-PCM 81.1, 41.4, 166.4; Penicillin V, C-PCM 78.0, 36.8, 186.0, and IEF-PCM 81.0, 36.7, 186.5.
assertions.reader_inference: Row-to-column mapping follows the table header (SCF, Gradient, Hessian under C-PCM then IEF-PCM) as printed.

assertions.value: The authors state that Q-Chem 6.1 does not support density fitting SCF with PCM models, so a standard SCF scheme is the reference, and that the PCM speedups should therefore be read as two factors: GPU speedup and density fitting speedup; the algorithms differ in the two programs.
quotes: Since Q-Chem 6.1 does not support density fitting SCF with PCM models, we use the standard SCF scheme as a reference.
Thus, the following speedups should be interpreted as two factors: GPU speedup and density fitting speedup.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the limit of the PCM comparison in Section 2.3.

assertions.value: The authors state that users can access four PCM variants (C-PCM, COSMO, IEF-PCM and SS(V)PE), that SMD adds CDS contributions with almost negligible cost, and that generalized Born models are not implemented in the current version.
quotes: users can access four variants of PCM models: C-PCM, COSMO, IEF-PCM, and SS(V)PE
Yet, the computational cost of these contributions is almost negligible.
Other types of implicit solvent models, such as generalized Born models, are not implemented in the current version.
assertions.certainty_reason: Feature scope stated in Sections 2.3 and 3.3.

assertions.value: The authors state that the PCM cavity surface is smoothed with SWIG methods, that atomic SASA, molecular SASA and CDS contributions use NWChem Fortran code and also a Python re-implementation using Lebedev quadrature that differs from the analytical formulation but usually negligibly for the CDS contribution, and that modified Coulomb radii with SMD18 parameters are employed.
quotes: The cavity surface of PCM models is smoothed using SWIG methods [68]
diverging from the analytical formulation in [70]. The difference is usually negligible for calculating the CDS contribution.
Modified Coulomb radii are employed with SMD18 [71]

assertions.value: The authors state that they re-engineered the PCM/SMD solvent models for GPU execution using Python, that further optimization to minimize memory requirements may be needed, and that PCM/SMD were also introduced in PySCF v2.4 with nuclear Hessian added in v2.6.
quotes: we have re-engineered the PCM/SMD solvent models for GPU execution using Python, recognizing the potential need for further optimizations to minimize the memory requirements
we also introduced PCM/SMD solvent models in PySCF v2.4 and added nuclear Hessian in PySCF v2.6

assertions.value: The authors state that PCM/SMD solvent models require solving the Poisson-Boltzmann equation in each SCF iteration, with cubic scaling in the number of grids on the molecular surface.
quotes: PCM/SMD solvent models require solving Poisson-Boltzmann equation in each SCF iteration.
is cubic-scaling with respect to the number of grids on molecular surface
assertions.reader_inference: The standard PCM formulation solves a surface integral equation for apparent surface charges, not the Poisson-Boltzmann equation; the description is the authors' own wording and was not checked against their code.

assertions.value: The authors report a torsional energy profile scan of Enzalutamide with 37 angles at 10 degree steps that entailed 1089 DFT evaluations, completed in 34,679.9 seconds, averaging approximately 32 seconds per DFT evaluation, with grid level 3 and density fitting on an A100-80G GPU.
quotes: at 10◦ step (37 angles in total)
This comprehensive analysis entailed 1089 DFT evaluations, with the entire scan completed in 34,679.9 seconds, averaging approximately 32 seconds per DFT evaluation.
All calculations in this subsection were performed using grid level 3 in PySCF with density fitting on an A100-80G GPU.
assertions.reader_inference: A single molecule and a single run; no comparison against a CPU code is given for this application.

assertions.value: The authors state that torsion scans require at least 24 independent constrained geometry optimizations for each proper torsion angle, each possibly needing 10-100 sequential quantum chemistry calculations, and that such scans have historically been restricted to small fragments with double-zeta basis sets.
quotes: they require at least 24 independent constrained geometry optimizations for each proper torsion angle in a molecule
each optimization might necessitate 10-100 sequential quantum chemistry calculations
Historically, such scans have been restricted to small molecule fragments, typically using small basis sets at the double-zeta level.

assertions.value: The authors report, for the interaction energy of Nirmatrelvir with a histidine residue, 42 single-point calculations with total wall times of 2370, 3082 and 5823 seconds for def2-SVP, def2-SVPD and def2-TZVPPD, and, with the counterpoise correction, 120 single-point calculations per basis with total wall times of 4020, 5510 and 11892 seconds, on an A100 GPU with grid level 3 and density fitting.
quotes: For the direct evaluation of interaction energy, 42 single-point energy calculations were conducted.
The total wall times for def2-SVP, def2-SVPD, and def2-TZVPPD bases were 2370, 3082, and 5823 seconds, respectively.
involving 120 single-point energy calculations for each base, with total wall times of 4020, 5510, and 11892 seconds, respectively
functional and grid level 3 in PySCF with density fitting on an A100-80G GPU.
assertions.reader_inference: The interaction energies themselves appear only in Figure 4(b), an image; the text gives timings only.

assertions.value: The authors report that the Li+ cluster calculations use the 6-311++G(3df,3pd) basis set with a cc-pVTZ-RI auxiliary basis for density fitting, IEF-PCM with UFF radii and dielectric constant 20.0, and the M06-2X functional with Grimme's D3 zero-damping dispersion; the clusters come from molecular dynamics of 2.25M LiFSI in DMC:EC at a weight ratio of 51:49.
quotes: All calculations are performed with 6-311++G(3df,3pd) basis set and cc-pVTZ-RI auxiliary basis for the density fitting technique.
The IEF-PCM with UFF radii was utilized for modeling solvent effects, with the dielectric constant being 20.0.
2.25M LiFSI(lithium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide) in DMC(dimethyl carbonate):EC(ethylene carbonate) with a weight percentage ratio of 51:49

assertions.value: The authors report in the cluster table the binding energies (eV) of nine Li+ clusters as -1.077, -1.020, -1.018, -1.004, -0.893, -0.857, -0.735, -0.656 and -0.065, listed for nine clusters.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer prints the cluster names and the energies in separate blocks; the pairing by order is the reader's. Section 3.1.3 describes the range as -0.065 eV to 1.078 eV, which has the opposite sign from Table 2 at the upper end, and Figure 6 gives -1.078 eV and -0.941 eV for Li+(DMC)(EC)(FSI-)2 whereas Table 2 lists -1.004 for that composition.

assertions.value: The authors state that most of the examined clusters have coordination number 4, that binding energies range from -0.065 eV to 1.078 eV, and that Li+/FSI- only clusters have the most positive binding energies compared with those containing solvents.
quotes: Most of the clusters we examined have a coordination number of 4
Their binding energies range from -0.065 eV to 1.078 eV
clusters composed solely of Li+ and FSI− exhibit the most positive binding energies compared to those containing solvents
assertions.reader_inference: Table 2 gives -1.077 as the most negative value, so the 'to 1.078 eV' end of the stated range disagrees in sign with the table and with Figure 6.

assertions.value: The authors report that two structures of a Li+ cluster with DMC, EC and two FSI anions have energies of -1.078 eV and -0.941 eV, and state that adequate geometric sampling is necessary for an accurate representation of solvation structure stabilities; they also state the examples are illustrative and not a complete study.
quotes: The energies of clusters in (a) and (b) are -1.078 eV and -0.941 eV, respecively.
adequate geometric sampling for DFT calculations is necessary for accurate representation of solvation structure stabilities
our examples in this section are merely illustrative and do not provide a complete study of the issue of Li+ ion solvation structures
assertions.reader_inference: The two Figure 6 energies span 0.137 eV for one composition.

assertions.value: The authors report that the CHELPG calculation in GPU4PySCF is approximately 10 times faster than CPU-based quantum chemistry software (Q-Chem), with Q-Chem using 64 cores and 128G memory and GPU4PySCF using 15 cores, 245G memory and one A100-SXM-80GB GPU, with consistent results under identical settings.
quotes: the calculation speed of CHELPG has been greatly improved approximately 10 times versus CPU-based quantum chemistry software [5]
The computations by Q-Chem used 64 cores and 128G memory, while GPU4PySCF used 15 cores, 245G memory, and one A100-SXM-80GB GPU.
Consistent results can be obtained when employing identical settings with Q-Chem.
assertions.reader_inference: The CHELPG comparison uses a different Q-Chem core count (64) from the 32 cores of Section 2.

assertions.value: The authors report that their CHELPG implementation uses a Cartesian grid with default spacing 0.3 angstrom and radial extent 2.8 angstrom, a smoothing function with Bondi radii (hydrogen changed to 1.1 angstrom), and the B3LYP functional with the def2-SVPD basis and density fitting.
quotes: Our implementation uses the Cartesian grid with the default spacing 0.3
and the radial extent of the CHELPG grid 2.8
the radius of hydrogen is changed to 1.1
All the calculations in this subsection are performed using B3LYP functional and def2-SVPD basis with density fitting used.

assertions.value: The authors state that NMR shielding constants are implemented with gauge-including atomic orbitals (GIAO), and show hydrogen shieldings of toluene computed with B3LYP, def2-TZVPP and the def2-universal-JKFIT auxiliary basis.
quotes: the NMR shielding constants are implemented using the gaugeincluding atomic orbitals [63] (GIAO)
This calculation employs the B3LYP functional, the def2-TZVPP basis set, and the def2-universal-JKFIT auxiliary basis set
assertions.certainty_reason: Implementation and setup stated in Section 3.2.2 and the Figure 8 caption.
assertions.reader_inference: No comparison of the shielding constants with experiment or with another program is given in the text.

assertions.value: The authors report that the three methyl hydrogens of toluene show differing chemical shifts in the calculation although, as they state, theoretically they should be identical, which they attribute to the geometrical configuration.
quotes: Due to the geometrical configuration, the three hydrogen atoms on the methyl group exhibit differing chemical shifts, although theoretically, they should be identical.
assertions.reader_inference: The numerical shifts appear only in Figure 8, an image.

assertions.value: The authors report that for neutral solutes the error in solvation free energies remains below 1 kcal/mol across protocols, decreasing with larger basis sets or higher rungs of Jacob's Ladder, and is comparable to Q-Chem and Gaussian; for ions the overall error is around 4 kcal/mol, with acetonitrile and dimethyl sulfoxide contributing most; SMD with Hartree-Fock generally outperforms B3LYP and M06-2X.
quotes: the error in solvation free energies consistently remains below 1 kcal/mol across various protocols (Table 3)
the overall error in solvation free energies is around 4 kcal/mol, with cases involving acetonitrile and dimethyl sulfoxide contributing significantly to this discrepancy
SMD calculations using Hartree-Fock generally outperform those utilizing DFT methods such as B3LYP and M06-2X
assertions.reader_inference: Table 3 values were printed scrambled by the text layer and were not entered cell by cell.

assertions.value: The authors report that the GPU4PySCF results use 2368 solvation free energies for neutrals and 362 for ions from the Minnesota Solvation Database, that Gaussian 03 results use 2346 and 332, that the reference data uncertainties are plus or minus 0.2 kcal/mol for neutral solutes and plus or minus 3 kcal/mol for ions, and that the database has been updated to version 2020 since the SMD publication.
quotes: 2368 solvation free energies for neutrals and 362 solvation free energies for ions are used for PySCF results
2346 solvation free energies for neutrals and 332 solvation free energies for ions are used for G03
The uncertainty of the reference data are ± 0.2 kcal/mol for neutral solutes and ± 3 kcal/mol for ions.
The database has been updated to version 2020 since the publication of SMD.
assertions.certainty_reason: Dataset sizes and reference uncertainties are stated in the Table 3 caption and Section 3.3.
assertions.reader_inference: The GPU4PySCF and Gaussian 03 sets differ in size, so the Table 3 comparison is not on identical solute sets. An ion error of about 4 kcal/mol is close to the stated ion reference uncertainty of 3 kcal/mol.

assertions.value: The authors report that for a subset of MOBH35 (reactions with bimolecular reactants or products removed) the mean absolute deviation of the reaction energy is 1.75 kcal/mol, similar to 1.7 kcal/mol reported for the entire database, and that re-optimized transition states are almost identical to the reference geometries, with 0.01 kcal/mol MAD in reaction energy between original and re-optimized geometries.
quotes: The average absolute deviation (MAD) of the reaction energy we calculated in the subset of MOBH35 is 1.75 kcal/mol, which is similar to MAD (1.7 kcal/mol) of the entire database reported in [78].
The difference of the reaction energy between the original geometry and re-optimized geometries is 0.01 kcal/mol in MAD.
The re-optimized transition states are almost identical to the geometries reported in [78].
assertions.reader_inference: The text gives the MAD as the paper's own label 'average absolute deviation'; the barrier height deviations appear only in Figure 9.

assertions.value: The authors state that the subset covers first, second and third row transition metals, that geometry and transition state optimizations use geomeTRIC, that they could not verify the transition states in modified geometries from a cited work and used the original geometries as initial guesses, and that the work provides no automated approach to reaction profile generation.
quotes: However, we are not able to verify the transition states in the modified geometries.
This work does not provide the automated approaches.
Both geometry optimizations and transition state optimizations are performed with geomeTRIC [79].
assertions.certainty_reason: Limits and setup stated in Section 3.4.1.

assertions.value: The authors state that oxidation and reduction potentials are computed through thermodynamic cycles, with 1.44 V subtracted to convert from the absolute scale to the Li/Li+ scale, and that their GPU4PySCF results are remarkably similar to those of a cited reference despite differing parameters; the largest discrepancy is the reduction potential of DMK, for which the same structure and method as the reference give 0.55 V, differing from the reported result.
quotes: Subtraction of 1.44 V converses from the absolute electrochemical scale to the Li/Li+ potential scale
despite differences in the computational approach and parameters from those described in the original literature, the results obtained are remarkably similar
the largest discrepancy lies in the reduction potential of the DMK molecule. Using the same structure and calculation method as Ref. [82], we get 0.55 V, which differs from the reported results.
assertions.reader_inference: The comparison is against another computational study, not against experiment. Individual potentials appear only in the Figure 10 bars.

assertions.value: The authors state that the acceleration ratio for oxidation-reduction potential calculations is determined by the lowest acceleration ratio among its parts (geometry optimizations in vacuum and solvent, and a Hessian in vacuum), but give no combined timing for the redox workflow.
quotes: the acceleration ratio for the calculation of oxidation-reduction potential is determined by the lowest acceleration ratio among these individual parts
assertions.reader_inference: This is a bound inferred from component speedups, not a measured end-to-end speedup.

assertions.value: The authors report for Anisole that the f minus Fukui function isosurface (isolevel 0.008) occurs mainly on the ortho- and para-position carbon atoms and less on meta, that condensed values using CHELPG charges agree, and that this matches the known ortho, para directing behaviour of the OCH3 group.
quotes: isosurface (isolevel 0.008) occurs mainly on the ortho- and para-position carbon atoms, and less in the meta-position
This result is consistent with organic chemistry knowledge that the -OCH3 group is an ortho, para director.
assertions.reader_inference: One molecule, qualitative agreement with textbook chemistry; no quantitative benchmark is given.

assertions.value: The authors state that atomic orbital (AO) evaluation on GPUs with GPU4PySCF achieves a hundredfold speed improvement (Figure 13: A100 GPU against multi-core CPUs, Benzene with the cc-pVDZ basis, for AO values, gradients and Hessian matrices).
quotes: With GPU4PySCF developed, AO evaluation can be efficiently performed on GPUs and achieves a hundredfold speed improvement as shown in Fig. 13.
Benzene with cc-pVDZ basis is used for benchmark.
assertions.reader_inference: The one-hundred-fold figure is stated in prose; the per-quantity ratios appear only in the Figure 13 image.

assertions.value: The authors report that integrating LapNet with GPU4PySCF gave approximately three times faster pretraining on the Benzene molecule.
quotes: by integrating LapNet [98] with GPU4PySCF, we achieved approximately three times faster pretraining on Benzene molecule
assertions.reader_inference: A single molecule; the three-fold figure is the pretraining step only, not the full variational Monte Carlo run.

assertions.value: The authors state that AO evaluation, invoked at every pretraining step of neural network wavefunction methods, is typically executed on CPUs and quickly becomes the computational bottleneck, partly through CPU-GPU data transfer.
quotes: AO evaluation, invoked at every ‘pretraining’ step, is typically executed on CPUs, which quickly becomes the computational bottleneck of the whole process

assertions.value: The authors state that from v1.0 GPU4PySCF drops the patching mechanism and redefines the same classes as PySCF, that a PySCF object is converted with to_gpu and back with to_cpu, and that they present a water-molecule example in which the CPU to GPU change is a single conversion call.
quotes: Starting from v1.0, GPU4PySCF drops the patching mechanism and explicitly redefines the same classes as in PySCF.
A PySCF object can be converted into a GPU4PySCF object with calling to_gpu function when the functionality is implemented on GPU.

assertions.value: The authors report, for a water molecule across functionals on rungs two to four of Jacob's Ladder, energy discrepancies relative to PySCF below ten to the power minus eleven Hartree (below the SCF convergence threshold of ten to the power minus ten), and 2-norm differences for gradients and Hessians below ten to the power minus seven Ha/Bohr and ten to the power minus six Ha/Bohr squared, with larger differences for range-separated functionals attributed to an ill-conditioned linear system in density fitting.

the 2-norm differences for gradients and Hessians are below 10−7 Ha/Bohr and 10−6 Ha/Bohr2, respectively
The large differences in range-separated functionals are due to solving ill-conditioned linear system in density fitting.
assertions.reader_inference: This is one molecule (water), with a def2-QZVPP basis and tolerance 10 to the power minus 12 in the Figure 14 caption.

assertions.value: The authors state that ECP contributions are calculated once in SCF using PySCF CPU routines for SCF, gradient and Hessian, that other DFT contributions remain GPU-accelerated for systems with ECP, that the cost is acceptable if the system has only a few heavy atoms, and that GPU acceleration of ECP is future work.
quotes: We reuse PySCF routines on CPU to calculate the ECP contributions in SCF, gradient, and Hessian.
The computational cost is acceptable if the system only has a few heavy atoms.
We leave the GPU acceleration of ECP as future work.

assertions.value: The authors state that dispersion corrections are calculated with dftd3/simple-dftd3 and dftd4 packages without GPU acceleration (rebuilt with OpenMP disabled), and that nonlocal corrections are optimized at the CUDA level because of their expensive computational cost.
quotes: these contributions are calculated with dftd3/simple-dftd3 and dftd4/dftd4 packages without GPU
Nonlocal corrections are carefully optimized at CUDA level due to its expensive computational cost.

assertions.value: The authors state that GPU4PySCF uses CuPy, cuTENSOR as the default tensor contraction engine, and a customized Python API for CUDA LibXC, which is experimental in libXC v6.2.
quotes: CUDA support is still experimental in the latest version of libXC (v6.2).
cuTENSOR is used as the default tensor contraction engine.

assertions.value: The authors state that GPU4PySCF includes only preliminary implementations of MP2 and CCSD methods, and that Table 4 lists the Hessian as finite-difference or CPU for several features.
quotes: Our work in GPU4PySCF includes preliminary implementations for MP2 and CCSD methods

assertions.value: The authors state that their implementations are certainly not optimal and that there are many current limitations, and list as future work: wavefunction methods, direct SCF integral schemes, periodic boundary conditions, multi-GPU use and mixed precision.
quotes: our implementations are certainly not optimal and there are many current limitations
In future work, it may be worth revisiting the integral scheme for direct SCF calculations.
assertions.certainty_reason: Limits and future work stated in Section 5.

assertions.value: The authors state that the low-level APIs of PySCF and GPU4PySCF are not fully compatible, so packages relying on low-level PySCF APIs cannot be directly accelerated with GPU4PySCF.
quotes: the low-level APIs of PySCF and GPU4PySCF are not fully compatible
packages relying on lowlevel PySCF APIs cannot be directly accelerated with GPU4PySCF

assertions.value: The authors state that sophisticated integral screening techniques in the CPU periodic boundary condition code may not transfer directly to GPU programs, and that new techniques are under development.
quotes: their techniques may not be directly transferable to GPU-based programs

assertions.value: The authors speculate that multi-GPU implementations perhaps can achieve greater parallel efficiency than 100% for large molecules.
quotes: Multi-GPU implementations perhaps can achieve greater parallel efficiency than 100% for large molecules.
assertions.reader_inference: Parallel efficiency above 100% is stated as a possibility only; no multi-GPU data are shown.

assertions.value: The authors state that GPU quantum chemistry faces three challenges: limited GPU memory, restricted CPU-GPU bandwidth and the complexity of GPU architecture.
quotes: Limited memory.
CPU-GPU communication.
Complexities of GPU architecture.
